title: Generalized nonsymmetric operads are the fibered objects of the incidence pattern
statement: Use simplicial sets, nerves, quasicategories and $\mathcal U$-small objects as in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], categorical patterns and $\mathfrak P$-fibered marked objects from [def-coef-categorical-pattern-fibrancy], and generalized nonsymmetric infinity operads in the convention of [lem-coef-marked-operadic-model-structures], in which no Kan condition on the fiber over $[0]$ is imposed. Let $B=N(\Delta^{\mathrm{op}})$ and let $I\subseteq B_1$ be the inert edges, the maps of $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$ opposite to inclusions of consecutive subintervals; $I$ contains every degenerate edge. For $n\geq0$ let $D_n$ be the finite category whose objects are the inert maps $\alpha:[n]\to[i]$ of $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$ with $i\in\{0,1\}$, and whose arrows $\alpha\to\beta$ are the inert maps $\gamma$ of $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$ with $\gamma\alpha=\beta$. Let $d_n:N(D_n)^{\triangleleft}\to B$ be the simplicial map induced by the functor sending the cone point to $[n]$, an object $\alpha:[n]\to[i]$ to $[i]$, the cone arrow to $\alpha$ to $\alpha$, and an arrow $\gamma$ to $\gamma$. Then every edge of $N(D_n)^{\triangleleft}$ maps into $I$, so $\mathfrak P_{\mathrm{gen}}=(B,I,\{d_n\}_{n\geq0})$ is a categorical pattern. For every $\mathcal U$-small marked simplicial set $(X,T)$ with a marking-preserving map $q:(X,T)\to(B,I)$, the following are equivalent: (a) $(X,T)$ is $\mathfrak P_{\mathrm{gen}}$-fibered; (b) $q$ is a generalized nonsymmetric infinity operad in the cited convention (inner fibration, cocartesian lifts of inert arrows, fiber comparison $X_{[n]}\to\lim_{\alpha\in D_n}X_{[i]}$ and incidence mapping-space comparisons equivalences), and $T$ is exactly the set of $q$-cocartesian edges lying over $I$. The case $n=0$, where $D_0$ is the one-object identity category, and empty $X$ are included.

source.place: Gepner–Haugseng, Enriched infinity-categories via nonsymmetric infinity-operads, Example 3.2.4(3) (a map to Delta^op is fibrant for the generalized pattern iff it is a generalized non-symmetric infinity-operad), read online (HTML v4) 2026-10-17; not archived in literature/.

proof.text: The nerve of any ordinary category is a quasicategory: an inner horn specifies its consecutive arrows and their composites, and associativity supplies the unique compatible simplex. Apply this to $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$, $D_n$, and the ordinary left cone of $D_n$. There are $n$ edge objects and $n+1$ vertex objects in $D_n$, with only the endpoint arrows besides identities, so it is finite. Consecutive-subinterval inclusions compose to such inclusions and include identities. Thus every cone leg and every factorization edge maps to $I$. The countable family of these finite cones is small in the fixed universe. These data meet exactly the categorical-pattern definition.

source.place: Definitions 3.1.13 and 3.2.3; Example 3.2.4(3), expanded agent argument

proof.text: In either direction the common first two clauses are that $q$ is an inner fibration admitting cocartesian lifts of inert arrows, with exactly those edges marked. Pull back along $d_n$. Inner-horn lifting is preserved by pullback: compose the base simplex with $d_n$ and use the filler for $q$. A $q$-cocartesian inert lift likewise remains cocartesian in the pullback by its horn property. Since all edges of the cone map to inert arrows, this gives a cocartesian fibration $q_n:E_n\to N(D_n)^{\triangleleft}$. Its classifying functor $\chi_n$ has value $X_{[n]}$ at the apex and $X_{[i]}$ at $\alpha:[n]\to[i]$, and all its arrows are the stated cocartesian transports, by straightening. For each $y\in X_{[n]}$ these transports give a coherent cocartesian section with apex $y$: the unique arrows from the initial cone vertex give the natural transformation from its constant functor to the identity, and applying $\chi_n$ and evaluating at $y$ gives this section under straightening. Conversely any cocartesian section has these transport values and compatibilities. Comparisons of such choices are equivalences by initiality of cocartesian lifts. A pullback-cocartesian edge over a cone edge is also $q$-cocartesian: it is locally cocartesian over that edge, and a global $q$-cocartesian lift already exists, so the local-global lemma applies.

source.place: Definitions 3.1.13 and 3.2.3; Example 3.2.4(3), expanded agent argument

proof.text: The cone of $\chi_n$ is precisely the comparison cone from $X_{[n]}$ to the incidence diagram $\alpha\mapsto X_{[i]}$. Small limits in $\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$ exist. To check the relative-to-a-point limit condition in pattern clause (iii), use the dual constant-diagram test: its bottom row consists of terminal spaces. The new mapping-from-a-constant-diagram lemma identifies its top right corner with the limit of the component mapping spaces. The representable limit criterion then says that this is exactly the usual limiting cone in $\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$. By the universal property of a limit, the specified cone is limiting exactly when its canonical comparison $X_{[n]}\to\lim_{\alpha\in D_n}X_{[i]}$ is an equivalence. Thus pattern clause (iii) and the generalized fiber clause agree.

source.place: Definitions 3.1.13 and 3.2.3; Example 3.2.4(3), expanded agent argument

proof.text: Fix a cocartesian section with image $s:N(D_n)^{\triangleleft}\to X$, apex $y\in X_{[n]}$, boundary $y_\alpha$, and a testing object $x\in X_{[m]}$. Apply the dual constant-diagram relative-limit test to $q$ and $s$. Apply the new mapping lemma to its upper and lower right corners, naturally with respect to $q$. The resulting square has upper row $$\operatorname{Map}_X(x,y)\longrightarrow\lim_{\alpha\in D_n}\operatorname{Map}_X(x,y_\alpha)$$ and lower row $$\operatorname{Map}_B([m],[n])\longrightarrow\lim_{\alpha\in D_n}\operatorname{Map}_B([m],[i]).$$ The horizontal arrows postcompose with the cone legs, so the lower arrow sends $\phi$ to $(\alpha\phi)_\alpha$. Mapping spaces in this ordinary nerve are the discrete Hom sets: in a right-pinched simplex every initial edge is an identity, and its only datum is the last arrow. This also identifies all coherence maps in the lower diagram.

source.place: Definitions 3.1.13 and 3.2.3; Example 3.2.4(3), expanded agent argument

proof.text: The square in Step 4 is a homotopy pullback exactly when its comparison becomes an equivalence on each homotopy fiber over $\phi\in\operatorname{Map}_B([m],[n])$: apply the homotopy-fiber detection lemma to the map from the upper-left corner to the path pullback, both over the lower-left corner with the identity as base map; the homotopy fiber of the path pullback over $\phi$ is the homotopy fiber of the right vertical map over $(\alpha\phi)_\alpha$. The space $\operatorname{Map}_B([m],[n])$ is discrete, so the comparison is a disjoint union of these fiber comparisons. Limits of spaces commute with homotopy pullbacks: maps into either iterated limit are exactly the same compatible cones, by the representable universal property. Its fiber comparison is therefore $$\operatorname{Map}^{\phi}_X(x,y)\longrightarrow\lim_{\alpha\in D_n}\operatorname{Map}^{\alpha\phi}_X(x,y_\alpha).$$ These homotopy fibers agree with the actual mapping-space fibers because the mapping map of an inner fibration is a Kan fibration. This is exactly the incidence mapping comparison in the generalized-operad statement. Step 2 supplies a cocartesian section for each $y$; all such sections give allowed coherent projection diagrams, and changing the lifts only changes them by the equivalences there. Hence requiring clause (iv) for every section is equivalent to requiring these incidence comparisons for every $x,y,\phi$.

source.place: Definitions 3.1.13 and 3.2.3; Example 3.2.4(3), expanded agent argument

proof.text: Steps 2, 3 and 5 identify all four pattern conditions with the generalized-operad clauses and the required marking, proving both implications. No Kan condition on $X_{[0]}$ has entered. For $n=0$ the only inert map to arity zero or one is the identity of $[0]$, so $D_0$ is the identity category and both comparisons are identities. For $n=1$ the identity of $[1]$ is initial in $D_1$ and the endpoint data introduce no extra arity-one condition. For empty $X$, every $D_n$ is nonempty, its all-empty fiber diagram has empty limit, and there are no $x,y$ or sections to test. Thus the fiber comparison is an equivalence of empty categories and the remaining conditions are vacuous. Degenerate marked arrows are already included by the cocartesian identity clause.
